Defining these compartments in a preclinical model could help connect clinical pharmacodynamic responses with the underlying vascular mechanisms and support further development of PACAP-targeted therapies. Using chronic cranial windows and head-mounted microscopy, we tracked meningeal vascular responses in freely moving mice. Nitroglycerin, levcromakalim, and PACAP38 each produced net vasodilation, yet the underlying responses were markedly heterogeneous and distributed differently across the vascular populations.

An adolescent peak in striatal dopamine availability is thought to contribute to the neuropsychiatric vulnerability. However, the lifespan trajectory of striatal dopamine release capacity is undefined in most species. Here, we measured lifespan trajectories of striatal dopamine in primates and rodents and identified a delayed developmental peak in adulthood and age-dependent changes in dopamine release regulation by GABA and acetylcholine across species.

https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Human stem cell neuroscience
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: In neuroscience, the most relevant human biology has often been the least accessible. Stem-cell-based models, such as organoids and assembloids, are opening ways to generate, assemble, probe, and perturb neural cells and circuits, helping define “stem cell neuroscience.” In this issue of Neuron, this and other reviews and commentaries discuss the current state of this emerging field.

https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Unbundling the ethical and social issues in human neural organoid research
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Cognitive evaluation of brain organoids and assembloids
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: The computational abilities of brain organoids and assembloids remain largely unexplored. https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Toward functional oversight of neural organoid research: A report from the 2025 Asilomar Conference
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: In November 2025, an international multistakeholder group convened at Asilomar, California, to address oversight of rapidly advancing neural organoid and assembloid research. https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: Human brain development is largely inaccessible to mechanistic investigation, and evolutionarily divergent programs cannot be fully modeled in other species. https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Neural organoid models of human brain evolution
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: Day et al. review how neural organoids enable experimental investigation of human brain evolution. https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.title: Advancing brain organoids from disease phenotypes to mechanisms and translation across developmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S08.summary: This review examines how human brain organoids are advancing studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, nervous system infections, and neurodegenerative diseases. https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: A cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia aligns 1.8 million nuclei from human, macaque, and marmoset into 61 cell types conserved over 76 million years. The atlas reveals that dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more evolutionarily constrained than direct and indirect pathway or striosome and matrix identity, identifies a distinct SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron type, and links regulatory sequence grammars and psychiatric risk variants to specific cell populations.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Using Slide-tags spatial transcriptomics across 19 human donors, this study shows that the striatum is organized into six molecularly distinct zones that are conserved in macaque and mouse, align with brain-wide projection inputs, and lose their transcriptional distinctiveness with age.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Single-cell analyses of the adult human striatum and prefrontal cortex reveal substantial inter-individual variation in cell-type abundance and gene expression. Most aspects of donor-associated cellular and molecular features recur across brain regions, while age and common genetic variation have distinct effects across cell types.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: A single-cell atlas of DNA methylation and 3D genome architecture across the human basal ganglia defines the regulatory signatures of its cell types, including a distinct striatal projection neuron subtype, and predicts cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks. Spatial transcriptomics further reveals interneuron types that differ between the striatal matrix and striosomes.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: A multimodal, integrative framework for understanding gene regulatory mechanisms across diverse cell types in the adult human brain. This framework helps elucidate how regulatory programs govern neuronal and glial functions, encode developmental trajectories, underlie neurological phenotypes, and change during evolution.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Dense multimodal profiling of the marmoset subcortex reveals how spatial context and gene regulatory programs jointly shape cell identity across the primate brain. By linking transcriptional states, chromatin accessibility, and anatomy, this atlas uncovers regulatory principles underlying spatial gradients, neuronal convergence, and evolutionary specialization.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Morphoelectric diversity and specialization of primate striatal neuron types
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Patch-seq in the macaque striatum links transcriptomic cell-type identity to neuronal form and function, revealing non-canonical spiny projection neurons, specialized interneurons, spatially organized morphoelectric gradients, and features that distinguish macaque from mouse neuron types.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Astrocyte diversity in the human basal ganglia reflects both large-scale brain identity programs and local microcircuit specialization. Integrated transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial analyses link these astrocyte populations to subgroup-specific regulatory features and enhancer logic, providing a framework for understanding and targeting astrocyte heterogeneity.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Cross-species single-cell profiling identifies molecular disruptions among striatal spiny projection neurons in genetically defined autism. D1 striosome spiny projection neurons are identified as the most affected, with altered synaptic and energy metabolism programs linked to reduced EGR1/EGR3 activity, partly reproduced by EGR1/EGR3 loss in organoids.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Single-cell and spatial profiling of the developing human basal ganglia show that their principal neurons, spiny projection neurons, mature through unusually synchronized epigenomic remodeling; that oligodendrocytes pass through a transient chromatin state during differentiation; and that spiny projection neurons carry an elevated genetic risk for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: Yang, Watkins et al. generate a 5.3 million cell transcriptomic atlas of the aging primate brain, which reveals that glia drive most age-related compositional shifts. These data uncover region-, cell-type-, and sex-specific molecular trajectories linked to neurodegenerative disease, providing key insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying brain aging and vulnerability.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: A comprehensive single-cell epigenomic atlas integrates four histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, the 3D genome, and the transcriptome, and resolves functional chromatin states of the adult mouse brain. This integrative framework, together with sequence-based deep learning, identifies active and repressive regulatory mechanisms and their dynamic deployment underlying cell-type-specific gene regulation.

https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092.summary: A Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) enables consistent creation of structural and cellular brain atlases and ontologies as well as the integration of multimodal data and samples across species.

https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fullte.title: Comamonas aquatica diet inhibits TIR-1/SARM1-induced axon degeneration by providing vitamin B12
https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fullte.summary: The gut microbiome influences neurodegeneration through poorly understood mechanisms. O'Connor et al. show that a Comamonas aquatica diet protects C. elegans motor axons from TIR-1/SARM1-induced degeneration via bacterial vitamin B12, which activates host METR-1/MTR and reduces neurotoxic homocysteine levels.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: Dynamin-2 mutations are associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) neuropathy; however, how these mutations affect neuronal function in vivo remains unclear. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: SOX7 and ERG reprograms neuroectoderm into microenvironmentally attuned brain endothelial cells that possess forebrain regional bias
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: Reliable human blood brain barrier (BBB) models are limited by a persistent problem of cellular identity: many protocols select cells for barrier or transporter properties rather than authentic, regionally specified brain endothelium. Here we show that constitutive expression of the transcription factors SOX7 and ERG converts human pluripotent stem cell derived epithelial barrier-forming cells into bona-fide vascular endothelial cells (SE rECs) whose transcriptome and proteome converge on primary human brain endothelium. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: HPV Oncogenes rewire DNA crosslink repair to create a PRIMPOL-dependent therapeutic vulnerability
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: Cisplatin-based chemoradiation is the standard of care for both HPV-negative (HPV-) and HPV-positive (HPV+) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), even though patients with HPV+ tumors have better treatment responses and a better prognosis. Understanding how HPV status shapes this response could guide alternative strategies that lower long-term toxicity. Using genome-wide CRISPR screens, we show that the genetic requirements for surviving chemoradiation diverge between HPV- and HPV+ HNSCC cells. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Enhancing pancreatic islet cell survival via NMDAR antagonist-driven ROR1 activation as revealed by phosphoproteomics
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: NMDA receptors (NMDARs) control function and survival not only of neurons, but also of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Since insufficient insulin secretion and beta cell death are key events during diabetes development, targeting NMDARs offers a therapeutic approach. Specifically, the NMDAR antagonist dextrorphan (DXO) increases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in clinical trials. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: CRISPR-based genetic modification is enabling curative, one-time treatments, but extending its use to more diseases will require increasing potency at low doses while avoiding unintended genomic modification. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Bloom unifies brain cell representations across modalities and contexts
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: Multimodal genomic datasets now profile mammalian brain cells across anatomical regions, developmental stages, disease states, and species. Learning shared representations that capture cellular diversity across these heterogeneous observations remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce Bloom, a transformer-based model that represents cells using gene expression, chromatin accessibility, or both. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: Diagonal integration seeks to align single-cell multi-omics datasets in which distinct modalities, such as RNA and protein, are measured in different cells. Unlike horizontal integration, these datasets lack direct cell--cell correspondences and complete feature mappings across modalities. Leading methods for weak-linkage integration often infer anchor cells between modalities by searching for cross-modal similarities through predefined feature links, then use these anchors to guide alignment. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Multimodal protein representations across human brain cell types
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.summary: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises diverse cell types whose molecular context shapes the roles of the proteins they express. Computational models offer a scalable way to study the roles of proteins across human brain cell types, with protein language models and interactome- or single-cell-based models capturing complementary information encoded in protein sequences and cellular network contexts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15049.summary: arXiv:2611.15049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humanity has long sought to explain natural phenomena. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15109.summary: arXiv:2611.15109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15831.summary: arXiv:2611.15831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14560.summary: arXiv:2611.14560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identifying a tumor's DNA mutations is central to cancer diagnosis and treatment, but distinguishing genuine mutations from sequencing artifacts is error-prone. In practice, genuine mutations are identified using fixed variant-allele-frequency (VAF) and depth thresholds which cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone where they overlap. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14568.title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14568.summary: arXiv:2611.14568v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14777.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14777.summary: arXiv:2611.14777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16425.title: RMIT-ADM+S at TREC RAG 2026: Research Agents, Retriever Ablations, and Open-Weight Replication
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16425.summary: arXiv:2611.16425v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We describe the RMIT-ADM+S team's participation in the TREC 2026 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) track using the ClimbMix corpus. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17015.summary: arXiv:2611.17015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28655.summary: arXiv:2605.28655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific research proceeds through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and revision. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Comment] Middle meningeal artery embolisation for chronic subdural haematoma
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Chronic subdural haematoma is among the most common reasons for neurosurgical admission, and its incidence keeps rising with population ageing and antithrombotic use. Evacuation relieves mass effect but leaves the inflamed, hypervascular outer membrane of the haematoma intact, and 5–30% of patients return for a second operation because of haematoma recurrence. Pharmaceutical agents aimed at targeting that membrane have not shown promising results: in Dex-CSDH, the proportion of patients undergoing reoperation fell to 1·7% with dexamethasone versus 7·1% with placebo, yet functional outcomes were worse.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Comment] Wise use of the optic nerve in multiple sclerosis diagnosis
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Optic neuritis is among the most common clinical manifestations of multiple sclerosis, being the initial presentation in around 25% of people and occurring at some point during the disease course in around 50%.1 Furthermore, post-mortem studies show near-ubiquitous pathological evidence of optic nerve involvement in multiple sclerosis, be it clinical or subclinical.2 Concerns regarding the sensitivity and specificity of different paraclinical tests to identify optic nerve involvement meant that the optic nerve was not added as a typical anatomical location for dissemination in space (DIS) in the 2017 McDonald criteria.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Comment] Dravet syndrome: modifying disease across the lifespan
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Dravet syndrome is a severe, rare form of genetic epilepsy that serves as a model disease for understanding monogenic (single gene) developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Affected individuals carry pathogenic variants in the sodium voltage-gated channel α subunit 1 gene, SCN1A, causing a channelopathy that presents with difficult-to-treat seizures and multiple morbidities, including intellectual disability.1 The emergence of genetic disease-modifying therapies is expanding treatment goals in Dravet syndrome from how many seizures can be prevented to which functions can be preserved or restored.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Correspondence] Bridging the gap between dementia risk factors and interventions
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Modifiable dementia risk factors are well established at the population level.1 Translating this epidemiological knowledge into effective action, however, requires evidence from interventional studies because established associations alone do not mean that modifying risk factors will reduce dementia incidence. In PENS,2 by contrast, in which patients underwent shunt surgery, the open-shunt setting increased gait velocity relative to the placebo valve setting by 0·21 m/s (95% CI 0·12 to 0·31; p<0·001) at 3 months.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [In Context] Patricia Pozo-Rosich: making migraine visible
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Patricia Pozo-Rosich was a teenager when she realised how lucky she was and decided to show her gratitude by making the world a better place. Her independent, vision-driven spirit has helped her to take pioneering professional paths. Once she sets her mind on a project, she brings to it perseverance and resilience matched with empathy and generosity. Today, she is head of the Neurology Department and director of the Migraine Adaptive Brain Center, Vall d'Hebron University Hospital, in Barcelona, Spain.

She considers the operating room her favourite classroom, where she continues to learn from patients, mentors, and colleagues. Her clinical interests include cerebrovascular and skull base surgery, alongside a growing interest in global neurosurgery and surgical education.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Increasing the number of women in neurology is an important step towards gender equity, but representation alone is not enough. Having women at the table benefits everyone: broader perspectives enrich the questions we ask, the solutions we consider, and the decisions we make. My experience in the American Academy of Neurology's Women Leading in Neurology (WLN) programme taught me that leadership is not about earning a seat at the table, but about how we use it and whom we bring with us.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Insight] Rethinking migraine prevalence in women and men
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Migraine is a common neurovascular disorder, with population-based studies consistently reporting a higher prevalence in women than in men, often with female-to-male ratios of 3–4:1. This sex difference is widely recognised and has shaped research agendas, diagnostic frameworks, and clinical thinking. It is frequently interpreted as reflecting underlying biological differences, particularly related to hormonal transitions across the life course. However, in a disorder without an objective diagnostic biomarker, observed prevalence is not solely a measure of biological susceptibility; it also reflects how migraine is experienced, reported, interpreted, and classified.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.title: [Review] Neuropathic pain: advances in diagnosis, mechanisms, and treatment
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laneu.summary: Neuropathic pain is chronic pain resulting from a lesion or disease of the peripheral or central somatosensory nervous system. Common examples include painful polyneuropathy (such as diabetic or chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy), trigeminal neuralgia, postherpetic neuralgia, and lumbosacral radiculopathy. Symptoms such as shooting or burning pain and allodynia can be screened for by using questionnaires, and neurophysiological, histological, or imaging assessments can establish the presence of a lesion.
